items.sentence: The NHS says they can take a few days to work.
items.note: search summary NHS laxatives: 2 to 3 days

items.sentence: Lactulose is described by the NHS as a laxative medicine to treat constipation.
StatPearls says lactulose is hardly absorbed by the gut, so its effects stay within the bowel.
Macrogol is not broken down in the body when taken by mouth; it hydrates hard stools, adds to their volume and triggers the reflex to pass them.
items.note: search summary; page attribution uncertain (pharmacology source)

items.sentence: Stomach ache, bloating, wind, feeling or being sick and diarrhoea are listed by the NHS for macrogol and lactulose.
Diarrhoea is particularly common with lactulose at higher amounts, and the NHS says reducing the amount may help.

The NHS lists muscle cramps or weakness, an irregular heartbeat and serious allergic reactions as uncommon side effects of lactulose; a serious allergic reaction needs a 999 call, and the other symptoms NHS 111 or the GP the same day.
items.note: NHS lactulose side effects; routes are site signposting

items.sentence: StatPearls says frequent diarrhoea from taking too much lactulose for too long can lower blood potassium.
The NHS says it is important to drink plenty of fluid when taking macrogol, to avoid dehydration.
The NHS says lactulose is given to younger children only on a doctor's recommendation, and macrogol to younger children only if prescribed.
